This page is generated from `_glossary.yml` — the same file the
`{{{< term key >}}}` shortcode reads for hover definitions in the chapters. A
definition lives in one place, so there is nowhere for it to drift.

### ATE {#term-ate}

*Average Treatment Effect — the mean effect across the whole population*

$\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)]$. The average causal effect over all
units. It answers "what happens if we treat everyone".


Also called: average causal effect in Hernán and Robins, who define it as a contrast of $\mathbb{E}[Y^{a=1}]$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y^{a=0}]$


Source: [@hernan2020; @imbens2015; @rubin1974]


See also: [ATT](#term-att), [ATU](#term-atu), [CATE](#term-cate), [potential outcomes](#term-potential-outcomes)

### ATT {#term-att}

*The effect on those who actually received treatment*

$\text{ATT} = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T = 1]$. Diverges from
{{< term ate >}} when the effect is heterogeneous and the treated are
not a random subset. In practice ATT is usually what gets estimated,
even though ATE is usually what gets asked about.


Also called: ATET, or the effect of treatment on the treated, in the econometrics literature


Source: [@angrist2009; @imbens2015; @facure2022]


See also: [ATE](#term-ate), [ATU](#term-atu), [CATE](#term-cate)

### ATU {#term-atu}

*The effect treatment would have had on those who did not receive it*

$\text{ATU} = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T = 0]$. Entirely counterfactual: it
is built from the outcome the untreated would have had under a treatment
none of them took. {{< term ate >}} is the size-weighted average of ATT
and ATU, so the three coincide only when the effect is homogeneous.


Also called: ATC, the effect on the controls


Source: [@imbens2015; @facure2022]


See also: [ATE](#term-ate), [ATT](#term-att)

### CATE {#term-cate}

*Effect conditional on covariates: a function of x, not a number*

$\text{CATE}(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]$. What you need when the
decision is about a specific unit rather than about the population.


Source: [@imbens2015; @facure2022]


See also: [ATE](#term-ate), [ATT](#term-att)

### confounder {#term-confounder}

*A common cause of both treatment and outcome*

A variable affecting both treatment assignment and the outcome. It
creates correlation between them in the total absence of a causal link.
The crucial asymmetry: a confounder must be **controlled for**, while a
collider must not be.


Source: [@hernan2020; @pearl2009]


See also: [selection bias](#term-selection-bias), [ignorability](#term-ignorability)

### counterfactual {#term-counterfactual}

*The unobserved half of the potential-outcome pair*

Whichever potential outcome did not happen. For a treated unit the
counterfactual is $Y_i(0)$. All of causal inference reduces to finding
something to stand in for the counterfactual.


Source: [@hernan2020; @holland1986]


See also: [potential outcomes](#term-potential-outcomes), [fundamental problem of causal inference](#term-fundamental-problem)

### fundamental problem of causal inference {#term-fundamental-problem}

*Both potential outcomes can never be observed for the same unit*

Holland's formulation, and his phrase: a unit-level causal effect is
unobservable because only one half of the pair is ever visible. It
follows that causal inference is always a **missing data** problem, not
a problem of describing the data you have.


Source: [@holland1986]


See also: [potential outcomes](#term-potential-outcomes), [counterfactual](#term-counterfactual)

### ignorability {#term-ignorability}

*Conditional independence of assignment from potential outcomes*

$(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp T \mid X$. Within each level of $X$, treatment is as
good as randomly assigned. The assumption is untestable: data can
neither confirm nor refute it, only subject-matter knowledge can argue
for it.


Also called: conditional exchangeability in Hernán and Robins (§3.2, where it sits beside positivity in §3.3 and consistency in §3.4 as one of three identifiability conditions), unconfoundedness in Imbens and Rubin, the conditional independence assumption (CIA) in Angrist and Pischke


Source: [@rubin1974; @imbens2015; @hernan2020; @angrist2009]


See also: [confounder](#term-confounder), [randomized experiment](#term-rct), [positivity](#term-positivity)

### positivity {#term-positivity}

*Every unit has a nonzero chance of landing in either group*

$0 < P(T = 1 \mid X = x) < 1$ for all $x$. If at some $x$ everyone is
treated or nobody is, there is no counterfactual available there, and
no method can repair that.


Also called: overlap, or common support, in the econometrics literature


Source: [@hernan2020; @imbens2015]


See also: [ignorability](#term-ignorability)

### potential outcomes {#term-potential-outcomes}

*The pair Y(0) and Y(1) for one unit: what would happen without treatment and with it*

Every unit has **two** outcomes defined: $Y_i(0)$, what would happen
without treatment, and $Y_i(1)$, what would happen with it. Exactly one
is ever observed. The causal effect for that unit is $Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$,
and it is fundamentally unobservable.


Also called: counterfactual outcomes, written $Y^{a}$ rather than $Y(a)$, in Hernán and Robins


Source: [@rubin1974; @holland1986; @imbens2015; @hernan2020]


See also: [counterfactual](#term-counterfactual), [fundamental problem of causal inference](#term-fundamental-problem), [ATE](#term-ate)

### randomized experiment {#term-rct}

*Treatment assigned by a coin flip, independently of potential outcomes*

The gold standard. Randomization makes assignment independent of the
potential outcomes, so a difference in means estimates {{< term ate >}}
without bias and without any modeling assumptions.


Source: [@hernan2020; @angrist2009]


See also: [ignorability](#term-ignorability), [selection bias](#term-selection-bias)

### selection bias {#term-selection-bias}

*Outcome gap caused not by treatment but by who ended up in which group*

Decomposition of the naive difference in means:
$\mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=0] = \underbrace{\text{ATT}}_{\text{effect}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=0]}_{\text{selection bias}}$.
The second term is how much the groups would have differed **with no
treatment at all**. Randomization sets it to zero by construction.


::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
The name is not shared across fields. This decomposition and its label
are the econometric usage. Hernán and Robins reserve *selection bias*
for bias created by conditioning on a common effect — a collider, or
selection into the study — and give it its own chapter (ch. 8), separate
from **confounding** (ch. 7), which is what they call the term above.
When reading across literatures, check which of the two is meant.
:::


Source: [@angrist2009; @facure2022; @hernan2020]


See also: [confounder](#term-confounder), [randomized experiment](#term-rct), [ignorability](#term-ignorability)

### SUTVA {#term-sutva}

*No interference between units, and one well-defined version of treatment*

Rubin's term, from his 1980 comment. Two requirements at once: (1) a
unit's outcome does not depend on the treatment assigned to other units;
(2) the treatment exists in a single version. Violated by network
effects, marketplaces, and anything where units compete for a shared
resource.


Also called: split by Hernán and Robins into *no interference* (Fine Point 1.1) and *consistency* (§3.4–3.5), which they treat as separate conditions rather than one acronym


Source: [@rubin1980; @imbens2015; @hernan2020]


See also: [potential outcomes](#term-potential-outcomes)
